analysis.one_liner: Gives internet users approval rights over how companies use their personal data.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to the Senate Commerce Committee the day it was introduced and never received a hearing, markup, or vote before the 116th Congress ended in January 2021.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have required broadband providers, websites, apps, and other online services to clearly disclose their privacy policies and to get your permission before using or sharing your data. Sensitive information — financial data, health records, Social Security numbers, precise location, and your browsing history — would need your explicit opt-in consent; less sensitive data could be used unless you opted out. It also barred companies from making service conditional on signing away privacy rights, put the Federal Trade Commission in charge of enforcement, and would have overridden state privacy laws.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary internet users — anyone with a broadband subscription, social media account, or smartphone app — who would gain the right to see, control, and withdraw consent for how their personal data is used, and could no longer be forced to waive privacy rights to get service.

how_it_helps.text: Covered services must give users clear, conspicuous notice of their privacy policies before sign-up, keep it persistently available, and give advance notice of material changes.

Users must give express opt-in consent before a provider uses or shares sensitive information: financial data, health information, children's data, Social Security numbers, precise geolocation, communications content, and web browsing or app-usage history.

For non-sensitive data, users can opt out of its use or disclosure, and providers must offer a simple, free mechanism to grant, deny, or withdraw consent at any time, which must take effect promptly and remain in force until changed.
Providers are barred from conditioning or terminating service on a user's refusal to waive privacy rights.
The Federal Trade Commission enforces the rules as unfair or deceptive practices, including over broadband providers, which are otherwise exempt from FTC jurisdiction as common carriers.

analysis.who_pays: Broadband providers, social media platforms, app makers, and the online advertising industry, which would lose unrestricted access to user browsing history and personal data that fuels targeted advertising, and would bear the cost of building consent systems and complying with FTC enforcement.

drawbacks.text: The bill preempts state privacy laws: no state could adopt or enforce its own rules on the privacy of user information for covered services, which critics would say locks in a single, potentially weaker federal standard and would override stronger state laws such as California's consumer privacy statute.

Non-sensitive data is used by default unless the user objects — consent is assumed from silence — and providers can use data without any approval for a range of purposes, including providing the service and protecting their own rights and property.

Enforcement rests solely with the FTC; the bill gives users no private right to sue violators themselves, and it nullifies existing Communications Act privacy regulations (except those covering emergency services) in favor of the new FTC framework.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill would hand internet users real, enforceable consent rights for the first time at the federal level, with browsing history treated as sensitive enough to require opt-in — stronger in that respect than most state laws. But its strengths come with a trade-off an honest supporter must acknowledge: it would wipe out state privacy protections in favor of one federal floor, leave non-sensitive data on an opt-out default, and depend entirely on FTC enforcement with no right for individuals to sue. Whether the net result helps consumers depends on how aggressively the FTC enforces it and how it compares to the state laws it displaces.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the Senate Commerce Committee the day it was introduced and sat there without a hearing, markup, or vote until the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Marsha Blackburn introduced the bill in the Senate on April 10, 2019.
The same day, it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation, which was its last action of record.
The bill drew two cosponsors, one Democrat and one Republican, and never advanced past committee referral.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Internet platforms, broadband providers, and the online data economy are better off because the bill died: they keep collecting and monetizing user data without federal consent requirements. Consumers gained nothing at the federal level, though the bill's preemption of state privacy laws never took effect either, leaving state laws like California's in place.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Internet platforms, broadband firms, and data brokers

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken; the bill's only demonstrated support was its Republican sponsor and two cosponsors split one from each party.

industries.note: The bill would require express opt-in consent before companies use or share browsing history and other sensitive data, cutting off much of the behavioral data that fuels targeted advertising. Consumers' interest in controlling their data runs directly against the industry's interest in monetizing it.

ISPs would lose their common-carrier exemption from FTC privacy enforcement and would need consent to use or sell customers' browsing data — protections similar in spirit to the FCC broadband privacy rules Congress repealed in 2017, which had never been in effect. Without it, they can continue monetizing customer usage data largely unchecked.

industries.industry: Websites, apps, and social media platforms
industries.note: Covered edge services would face new notice, consent, and compliance costs, including for sensitive data like precise location and app-usage history. But the bill's preemption of state privacy laws would replace a patchwork of state rules — including stronger ones like California's — with a single federal standard and a relatively modest opt-out default, which large platforms have historically welcomed.
